bib.title: Education (Chapter 12)
bib.venue: The Data Warehouse Toolkit (book chapter, pp. 243-254)

question: How are an admissions pipeline, registration, attendance, facility use and non-events modelled dimensionally for a university?
contributions: Applicant pipeline as an accumulating snapshot
Factless fact tables (event and coverage) for registration, attendance, facilities and promotions
Techniques for analysing events that did not occur

results.claim: An accumulating snapshot row is one complete history, revisited and changed on each event, and fits short-lived processes.
results.setup: Kimball chapter 12, university case study, design guidance not measured
results.quote: Each row is revisited and changed whenever something happens.

results.claim: The applicant pipeline grain is one row per prospective student, with role-playing date keys using surrogate keys for unknown dates at first load.
results.setup: Kimball chapter 12, university case study, design guidance not measured
results.quote: The grain of the accumulating snapshot to track the applicant’s lifecycle is one row per prospective student.

results.claim: A factless fact table has keys but no measured facts; counts replace sums.
results.setup: Kimball chapter 12, university case study, design guidance not measured
results.quote: There are no measured facts! We call these factless fact tables.

results.claim: Registration grain is one row per registered course by student and term; the term dimension must conform to the calendar date dimension.
results.setup: Kimball chapter 12, university case study, design guidance not measured
results.quote: The grain of the fact table would be one row for each registered course by student and term.

results.claim: Counting any key in a factless table gives the same answer; COUNT DISTINCT is needed for unique instances.
results.setup: Kimball chapter 12, university case study, design guidance not measured
results.quote: you can count any key and still get the same answer

results.claim: A constant registration count of 1 is added for readable SQL and so aggregates have a real column to roll up.
results.setup: Kimball chapter 12, university case study, design guidance not measured
results.quote: we will need a real column to roll up to meaningful aggregate registration counts.

results.claim: A coverage table has a row for every facility per hourly block per term whether used or not.
results.setup: Kimball chapter 12, university case study, design guidance not measured
results.quote: regardless of whether the facility is

results.claim: Explicit rows for non-events suit attendance (no-shows, attendance 1 or 0) but not flights not taken.
results.setup: Kimball chapter 12, university case study, design guidance not measured
results.quote: creating rows for events that didn’t happen is ridiculous in many situations

results.claim: Promotion coverage table answers 'promoted but did not sell' by set difference against sales; it is far smaller than zero rows in the sales fact.
results.setup: Kimball chapter 12, university case study, design guidance not measured
results.quote: the set difference between these two lists of products is our answer.

results.claim: NOT EXISTS avoids design work but is slow, tool-limited and misses products that never sold in the window.
results.setup: Kimball chapter 12, university case study, design guidance not measured
results.quote: we’ll miss products that didn’t sell at all during the extended time frame.

results.claim: Multidimensional OLAP cubes handle sparsity so non-events are analysable without stored zeroes.
results.setup: Kimball chapter 12, university case study, design guidance not measured
results.quote: Multidimensional online analytical processing (OLAP) databases do an excellent job

limits: Design guidance from a hypothetical university; no measurements or benchmarks.
Non-event SQL examples are 2002-era and relational/OLAP only.
Page 246 extract contains scan noise only.
practices: Use an accumulating snapshot for short-lived processes with standard milestones (applicant, grant proposal); p.244, p.246.
Model each milestone date as a role-playing date dimension with surrogate keys for unknown dates; p.246.
Model event tables as keys-only factless facts; p.248.
Add an always-1 count column for readable SQL and aggregates; p.249.
Add real facts (tuition, credit hours, grade) only if consistent with the grain, which ends factlessness; p.249.
Use a coverage table with a row for every possible combination, used or not, to analyse non-use; p.249.
Make the term dimension conform to the calendar date dimension with identical common attributes; p.247.
Treat frequently changing student attributes (major, class level) as minidimensions; p.248.
Add explicit zero rows only when non-events share dimensionality and are few; p.251.
Prefer a promotion coverage table to zero rows or NOT EXISTS for unsold promoted items; p.251-252.

terms.definition: A single row represents the complete history of something; multiple dates for milestones; revisited and changed when something happens.
Events often are modeled as a fact table containing a series of keys, each representing a participating dimension in the event.
Factless fact table with a row for each combination that could occur, used or not, e.g. facility utilization or promotion coverage.
